segments.title: Japan joins Britain after France falls
segments.body: The scenario puts Japan beside Britain and the Free Powers on 25 June 1940, after France falls. Its essential departure from history is that the Second Sino-Japanese War never begins in 1937. Japanese-American relations would still be poor, and avoiding war in China would not remove the prospect of a later Pacific conflict. Some Japanese leaders considered a long war against America unsustainable because Japan lacked the infrastructure and operational depth to fight it alone. A further proposal was to make America declare war, hoping this would weaken domestic support for the conflict there. These constraints frame the proposed choice to join Britain after France falls.

evidence.note: Japan joins Britain and the Free Powers on 25 June 1940 under the assumption that the Second Sino-Japanese War never begins.
Poor Japanese-American relations, proposed approaches to war, and Japan's limited capacity for a prolonged conflict remain constraints.
The counterfactual turns France's fall into the occasion for Japan to join Britain.

segments.summary: The scenario starts from a narrow counterfactual: no Second Sino-Japanese War, France falls, and Japan chooses Britain in June 1940.

segments.title: Akagi and Soryu form Japan's proposed carrier contribution
segments.body: Japan's carrier contribution depends on refits, training, and the ships retained for home defence. Hosho cannot operate the latest aircraft, while Kaga remains in refit until November 1940 and would need further preparation before deployment. Ryujo's stability problems make her an unattractive choice for European waters, and Hiryu is still working up after commissioning in 1939. The Shokaku and Hiyo classes are unavailable, and Taiho has not yet been laid down. The proposed deployment sends Akagi to the Atlantic and Soryu to the Mediterranean while keeping other carriers near Japan because distrust of America continues. Kaga might later join the Atlantic forces, although doubts about her speed could instead keep her at home and release Hiryu for service abroad. Keeping Soryu in the Mediterranean also leaves her closer to Japan.

evidence.note: Carrier readiness, refits, stability, and aircraft compatibility restrict the initial Japanese contribution.
Several carriers remain near Japan while Akagi and Soryu deploy according to availability and operating conditions.

segments.summary: Refit schedules, operating conditions, and home-defence commitments lead to a proposed deployment of Akagi to the Atlantic and Soryu to the Mediterranean.

segments.title: Kongos and Nagatos reinforce different Allied fleets
segments.body: Japanese capital-ship availability rules out sending the entire battle fleet. Two or perhaps three Kongo-class ships could deploy first, with one supporting Force H and the others strengthening the Home Fleet against German breakouts. Nagato and Mutsu would take longer to prepare, but their 16-inch guns make them valuable in northern waters, while older or unfinished battleships remain in Japan. The opening estimate allows them to head out in late October or early November after a June decision. Cruisers and destroyers would accompany the formation, and the detachment would reinforce Cunningham's Mediterranean command. A Japanese admiral and ships would need working Allied communications and command arrangements. British and Japanese forces had pointed guns at one another in 1939, and the January 1940 Asama Maru incident had sharpened tensions only months before the proposed alliance.

evidence.note: Kongo-class readiness and the proposed Force H and Home Fleet split, with Nagato-class ships following later.
Upgraded Kongo-class ships could answer Germany's fast capital ships in 1940; the unfinished Yamato class would be unavailable.
The initial estimate sends Nagato and Mutsu out in late October or early November, while two carriers, two to three Kongos, cruisers, and destroyers form the earlier contribution.
The 1939 Anglo-Japanese confrontation and January 1940 Asama Maru incident complicate renewed cooperation.

segments.summary: Speed, readiness, and gun power send one Kongo toward Force H, other fast ships toward the Home Fleet, and the Nagato class toward Atlantic blocking duties.

segments.title: Rebuilt Kongos complicate German Atlantic breakouts
segments.body: More carriers at Taranto could reduce the later demand for heavy capital ships in the Mediterranean and leave them available to contain German breakouts. The proposed match-up gives upgraded Kongos a useful role against Scharnhorst and Gneisenau. Some reconstructions are judged to have carried them across the boundary into fast battleships, although Japanese treatment of the ships still reflects their battlecruiser role. Stronger Allied forces might discourage Scharnhorst and Gneisenau from operating independently and leave them available for a later sortie with Bismarck. That possibility strengthens the case for sending Nagato and Mutsu to the Home Fleet. Yamato and Musashi would still be unavailable for the initial deployment.

evidence.note: Mediterranean carrier reinforcement, the classification of rebuilt Kongos, and the possibility of Germany concentrating its capital ships for a later breakout.

segments.summary: Reconstructed Kongos could help contain Germany's fast capital ships, while a stronger Mediterranean carrier force releases heavier ships for the Home Fleet.

segments.title: Japanese reinforcements need a place in Allied command
segments.body: Cruisers and destroyers would accompany Japan's capital ships according to availability, and some cruisers could hunt surface raiders. The detachment would be large enough to bring its own admiral while fitting into the Allied command structure. Cunningham would retain his Mediterranean command. Communications and coordination would need practical arrangements between the two navies. Their recent confrontations, including the January 1940 Asama Maru incident, make cooperation difficult, although the scenario assumes those problems can be overcome.

evidence.note: Cruiser and destroyer support, a Japanese admiral, retained British command, communications, and recent Anglo-Japanese confrontations.

segments.summary: Japan's detachment would bring an admiral and supporting ships, requiring practical communications and command arrangements with British forces.

segments.title: Yonai gives Japan an old-alliance option
segments.body: Mitsumasa Yonai gives the proposed alliance a figure with influence across competing institutions and factions. His standing with the emperor, Buddhist groups, and military leaders supports the scenario's assessment that he could withstand opposition to a change in policy. His later role in securing the navy's surrender, together with a credited contribution to the foundations of the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force, forms part of that assessment. Yonai opposed war with America because he considered it unwinnable. Without the Second Sino-Japanese War, the scenario gives him more freedom to pursue an alliance that supplies resources and time to strengthen Japan. Renewed cooperation would also provide Britain with forces it urgently needs.

evidence.note: Yonai's influence with the emperor and competing groups, his role in naval surrender, and a credited contribution to later maritime institutions.
Yonai's opposition to war with America and the proposed exchange of Japanese support for access to British imperial resources.

segments.summary: The scenario uses Yonai's influence and opposition to war with America to explain a possible return to Britain's side.

segments.title: Japan seeks time and resources through its old alliance
segments.body: Fighting beside Britain is proposed as a way to buy time for Japan's internal affairs and its difficult relationship with America. British contacts could help mediate an accommodation, and eventual gains from Italy's empire provide another inducement. An imagined announcement presents intervention as renewed loyalty to a traditional ally and invokes the Washington and London naval treaties as part of that public justification. Support from the emperor could strengthen Yonai's position, although involving the emperor too deeply in politics carries its own difficulty. The plan also envisages an army corps for North Africa. These are Japanese strategic aims within the scenario, with renewed friendship supplying the public explanation. The proposal assumes that American pressure on Japan would become harder to separate from interference with Britain's war effort.

evidence.note: British mediation, Japanese strategic aims, an imagined alliance announcement invoking naval treaties, imperial support, and the proposed American diplomatic dilemma.

segments.summary: The imagined alliance gives Japan time to manage its internal problems and relations with America while offering territorial and diplomatic gains.

segments.title: Warships arrive before Japan's land and air reinforcements
segments.body: Japan could send bombers and an expeditionary corps as well as warships, although deploying land forces and aircraft would take longer. Ships bring accommodation, food, maintainers, and much of their support with them, while troops and aircraft require overseas bases and supply chains. Ammunition and fuel still have to reach the naval force, with Britain able to help meet its fuel requirements. North Africa offers the easiest destination for the land and air contribution through a supply route the scenario treats as uninterrupted. The absence of war with Japan also releases Indian Army and other forces that historically fought in Burma. Japanese carrier and aviation development is assumed to remain broadly similar despite the missing combat experience in China. Japan's bomber force is compared with the German and Italian formations, in contrast to British and American emphasis on mass heavy bombers.

evidence.note: Japanese bombers and an expeditionary corps need overseas bases and support, while ships bring much of their accommodation and maintenance capacity with them. The bomber-force comparison distinguishes Japanese, German, and Italian formations from British and American heavy-bomber forces.
A secure route into North Africa and the release of Indian Army forces otherwise committed to Burma.

segments.summary: Self-contained warships can deploy before troops and aircraft, while secure routes to North Africa and the absence of fighting in Burma increase the available Allied forces.

segments.title: Shipping losses expose India's dependence on sea transport
segments.body: Avoiding war with Japan could reduce the severity of the Indian famine by keeping sea routes safer and making more merchant ships available. Crop failures could still occur, so the scenario does not assume that famine disappears. American and Japanese ships could help fill transport gaps that become harder to cover when wartime losses and Atlantic commitments absorb shipping. One interpretation places particular weight on earlier failures to fund Indian railways and freight infrastructure. Its criticism of Churchill concerns his earlier role as chancellor and the decision to leave railway funding to a colonial government that said it lacked the money. The argument connects the later transport crisis with those earlier investment decisions.

evidence.note: Safer transport and additional merchant vessels could ease shortages without eliminating crop failures.
An interpretation of famine vulnerability focused on earlier railway funding decisions and the allocation of financial responsibility.

segments.summary: Safer shipping could ease famine shortages, while the explanation of transport vulnerability places weight on earlier railway investment decisions.

segments.title: Churchill must integrate Japan without excluding America
segments.body: Japan's proposed entry creates a diplomatic and coalition-command problem for Britain. Churchill would need to establish what Tokyo wanted and how Japanese units would operate with British forces. In this scenario, Japan seeks time to strengthen its forces and influence over a postwar division of spheres of influence. A meeting at Cairo or Alexandria could bring Churchill and Yonai together with Free Allied leaders and a senior American representative. American participation would make the talks more open and leave a route into the broader alliance. Britain's immediate need for military help would therefore have to be managed alongside American concern about exclusion from a future settlement.

evidence.note: Churchill would welcome Japanese help while worrying about Tokyo's sphere-of-influence ambitions, integrating its forces, managing the American reaction, and keeping any meeting visibly above board.
The difficulties of managing the alliance and the parliamentary circumstances surrounding Churchill's succession.

segments.summary: Japan's proposed alliance would leave Churchill coordinating Japanese forces while keeping American representatives involved in the negotiations.

segments.title: Churchill and Halifax at the succession meeting
segments.body: The account of Churchill's succession begins with Conservative strength in Parliament, which restricted the choice of the next prime minister. Churchill and Halifax were both present when Chamberlain raised the question of who would succeed him. Halifax offered to serve under Churchill, while Churchill remained silent. Their responses are presented as part of the explanation for how the succession was settled.

evidence.note: Conservative parliamentary strength and the account of Halifax offering to serve under Churchill during the succession discussion.

segments.summary: Parliamentary arithmetic and the exchange between Chamberlain, Halifax, and Churchill frame the account of the premiership changing hands.

segments.title: Japanese entry could influence French colonial allegiances
segments.body: Japanese forces would not reach Europe in time to change Mers-el-Kebir directly. Their entry into the war could nevertheless affect the position of French colonies after France's fall. Some colonial authorities could fear that Japan would occupy them if they remained outside the Free French movement. Concern that Japan might retain those territories could encourage them to join the Free French. These colonial choices remain possibilities within the scenario.

evidence.note: Japanese arrival would be too late for Mers-el-Kebir, while fears of occupation could encourage French colonies to support the Free French.

segments.summary: Japanese forces would arrive too late to change Mers-el-Kebir directly, while fear of occupation could affect French colonies' choices.

segments.title: Pacific security releases Dominion forces
segments.body: Japanese entry on Britain's side would release forces otherwise held for Pacific defence. John Curtin and Peter Fraser are named in connection with Australian and New Zealand concern about Japan and control over the deployment of their forces. Their countries would still retain some troops at home and watch Japanese intentions, but more formations could go to the Mediterranean and North Africa. Canada would have less reason to send a brigade to Hong Kong, and reinforcements destined for Singapore and Malaya could also move west. Confidence in the alliance would increase once Japanese forces were committed to combat, because those units would be harder to withdraw suddenly. The gain would include British Empire troops made available by the changed strategic position as well as the Japanese forces themselves.

evidence.note: Australian, New Zealand, Canadian, Singapore, Malaya, and Hong Kong commitments could shift toward North Africa and Europe.
Home-defence precautions would continue, but a Japanese force already in combat would be harder to withdraw suddenly.

segments.summary: Japan's belligerence on Britain's side reduces pressure on Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Malaya, and Hong Kong, releasing more troops for North Africa and Europe.

segments.title: A peaceful Pacific supports trade and supplies for North Africa
segments.body: Continued earnings from Malaya and the sterling area would help Britain meet the costs of war in this scenario. Japan could also remain a market for raw materials from the British Empire. American goods could sail from the west coast across the Pacific and Indian Oceans to supply North Africa. That route would take longer than crossing the Atlantic. Without a Pacific war, however, merchant ships could sail independently through those oceans with less demand for convoy escorts. Atlantic and Mediterranean shipping would still face their own wartime requirements.

evidence.note: Malayan and sterling-area finances and Japanese demand for British Empire raw materials.
A longer but safer American west-coast route across the Pacific and Indian Oceans, with reduced convoy requirements.

segments.summary: Malayan earnings, Japanese demand for raw materials, and a safer ocean route could ease Britain's economic and shipping pressures.

segments.title: American Far Eastern interests complicate isolationism
segments.body: The counterfactual explores several different pressures for American involvement in an Anglo-Japanese alliance. Its proposed public presentation as a defence of the free world is political messaging, and Japan's place in that description is explicitly questioned. Concern about an exclusive British-Japanese partnership could combine with national prestige, sympathy for Britain, or opposition to fascism. Opposition to a European war would not necessarily remove American interest in the Far East. The proposed route to wider cooperation depends on some opponents of European intervention deciding that participation would prevent Britain and Japan from arranging Asian affairs without them. Other isolationists would still oppose joining the war.

evidence.note: Proposed alliance messaging, different American reasons for involvement, and the distinction between opposition to European intervention and interest in the Far East.

segments.summary: The counterfactual links American pressure for participation to concern about exclusion from a British-Japanese settlement in the Far East.

segments.title: A limited naval commitment offers one route to American entry
segments.body: A limited naval commitment is one proposed route to American participation in this counterfactual. The earliest suggested deployment to the Mediterranean or Home Fleet is late October or early November, provided Roosevelt could obtain support for ships without ground troops. The estimate then allows a longer delay of about a year in the slower version of the scenario. Marines are considered a possible further compromise while broader ground-force commitments remain difficult. Another proposed route is the continued eastward extension of Atlantic neutrality patrols, increasing the chance of a confrontation with Germany. The absence of the Second Sino-Japanese War would also remove a recent source of hostility between the United States and Japan.

evidence.note: Conditional naval deployment by late October or early November, with a longer delay of about a year also considered.
Eastward neutrality patrols and a possible naval or Marine commitment while wider ground-force deployment remains difficult.
The removal of the Second Sino-Japanese War changes the background to American-Japanese relations.

segments.summary: The counterfactual considers a naval commitment and expanded Atlantic patrols as possible routes to American participation.

segments.title: Pearl Harbor preparation and commanders' access to intelligence
segments.body: The Pearl Harbor interpretation rejects the suggestion that the attack was deliberately arranged. Its explanation instead concerns the positioning of forces, inadequate preparation, and restrictions on commanders' access to information. Earlier commanders' use of that information to question the deployment is part of the criticism. These are presented as failures of readiness and intelligence access, with an expectation of safety contributing to the problem.

evidence.note: Rejection of Pearl Harbor conspiracy claims and an interpretation focused on force positioning, preparation, and commanders' access to information.

segments.summary: The explanation of Pearl Harbor focuses on preparedness and access to information while rejecting a deliberately arranged attack.

segments.title: Suez becomes the Axis pressure point
segments.body: Germany and Italy would face a more concentrated opposing fleet if Japan joined Britain. Britain could reduce its Far Eastern requirements and deploy more ships to the Mediterranean and Home Fleet. For Italy, reaching Alexandria or blocking Suez would offer a way to obstruct Japanese reinforcements arriving through the Indian Ocean. Japanese ships could still enter through Gibraltar, but that route would be harder to sustain. A secure Indian Ocean would also let Britain relocate ships and mobile support facilities closer to the Mediterranean. The timing limits the Axis response: German U-boat strength has yet to reach its later peak, the Greco-Italian War historically begins in October 1940, and the Afrika Korps deploys in February 1941.

evidence.note: The Axis reaction as strategically bad, with Japan reinforcing the Mediterranean and Home Fleet while Britain can reduce Far East commitments.
Blocking Suez or Alexandria could obstruct the direct reinforcement route, while entry through Gibraltar would remain possible.
The Indian Ocean becoming a safe holding area for British and Japanese assets, including mobile infrastructure from Singapore.
In June 1940 the U-boat force was limited, while the Greco-Italian War and Afrika Korps deployment still lay in the historical future.

segments.summary: Japan's entry makes the Mediterranean and Suez central because the Indian Ocean becomes a safer Allied support area.

segments.title: A secure Indian Ocean allows mobile fleet support to move west
segments.body: A secure Indian Ocean could provide a holding area for ships supporting the Mediterranean war. Capital ships could pass south through Suez when they were not needed at Alexandria. This could make them harder for frogmen to reach, although their return through the canal might become easier to predict. Floating docks and other mobile support facilities could move from Singapore because Britain would no longer need the same capacity for a potential Far Eastern fleet. Japan could bring its own supporting infrastructure as well. These arrangements depend on the different operational conditions of the counterfactual.

evidence.note: Capital ships could wait beyond Suez, with a possible reduction in frogman exposure and potentially more predictable canal movements.
British mobile infrastructure could move from Singapore, while Japan could bring its own support facilities.

segments.summary: Capital ships and floating docks could shift closer to the Mediterranean when Britain no longer needs to prepare for a Pacific naval war.

segments.title: The 1939 Soviet-Japanese war still shapes Stalin
segments.body: Removing the Second Sino-Japanese War does not necessarily erase the 1939 fighting between Japan and the Soviet Union. That Soviet-Japanese clash remains plausible in this timeline. Its outcome is still part of Stalin's strategic calculation and could affect the timing of the Soviet move into Poland. Stalin would evaluate the new Anglo-Japanese coalition against the memory of a recent war in the Far East.

evidence.note: The 1939 Soviet-Japanese conflict is retained as a possible event in this scenario and as a factor in Stalin's timing in Poland.

segments.summary: Even without war in China, the 1939 Soviet-Japanese conflict may still occur and affect Stalin's timing in Poland.

segments.title: Force H gains speed while the Home Fleet gains weight
segments.body: The proposed deployment sends Haruna to Force H and Kongo and Kirishima to the Home Fleet, with Akagi supporting Atlantic operations and Soryu going to the Mediterranean. Hiei would need to finish working up after her January 1940 reconstruction and is expected to join the Home Fleet once available. Nagato and Mutsu would take longer to prepare, with their deployment projected for 1941. These choices address Britain's shortage of fast capital ships for Home Fleet operations and Force H. Renown and Haruna, supported by Ark Royal, would provide Force H with a strong pair of fast capital ships. Supporting cruisers and destroyers could be drawn from both navies.

evidence.note: Carrier and Kongo-class readiness determine Mediterranean and Home Fleet assignments.
Italy's operational battle fleet, fuel restrictions, and the attention given to German warships.
Fast capital ships would reinforce the Home Fleet and a Force H centred on Renown, Haruna, and Ark Royal.

segments.summary: A detailed allocation sends Soryu and Haruna toward the Mediterranean, Akagi and other Kongos toward Atlantic duties, and the Nagatos toward the Home Fleet.

segments.title: Italian fleet strength receives less attention than German battleships
segments.body: Japanese deployments to the Atlantic carry an anticipated desire to fight Germany after missing that opportunity during the First World War. Italy nevertheless has the stronger and more balanced surface fleet in this comparison. Germany generally has only two of its modern capital ships available together because losses and refits limit simultaneous readiness. Italy can draw on six battleships and usually has three or four available, although fuel and Allied action restrict operations further. The 1940 scenario treats all six Italian battleships as ready, operating in a Mediterranean where friendly control of the air cannot be assumed. The greater attention given to Bismarck, Tirpitz, Scharnhorst, and Gneisenau is attributed to status and historical narrative.

evidence.note: Japanese interest in fighting Germany, Italian and German fleet availability, Mediterranean air conditions, and the prestige of German capital ships.

segments.summary: Italy's larger and more balanced fleet is contrasted with the prestige attached to fighting Germany's better-known capital ships.

segments.title: Soviet neutrality under pressure from Britain and Japan
segments.body: An Anglo-Japanese naval coalition would confront Soviet interests from opposite directions while the Soviet fleet lacked comparable reach. Recent fighting with Japan and longstanding suspicion of Britain would complicate cooperation with either power. The scenario considers Soviet alignment with the coalition, closer alignment with Germany, and continued neutrality. It develops a wait-and-see course, with Stalin delaying a commitment while the strategic situation changes. If Germany still invaded the Soviet Union, a neutral Soviet position beforehand could benefit the Allies. Avoiding commitments in North Africa, Greece, and possibly Yugoslavia could permit an earlier invasion, but a change to German plans is uncertain.

evidence.note: The combined British and Japanese navies would threaten Soviet interests from opposite directions.
The scenario compares coalition membership, support for Germany, and continued Soviet neutrality.
Reduced German commitments in Greece and North Africa could alter the timing of an invasion of the Soviet Union.

segments.summary: The scenario considers how pressure from British and Japanese naval power could affect Soviet neutrality and the timing of Germany's eastern campaign.

segments.title: German commanders share responsibility for strategic planning
segments.body: The interpretation of German strategy assigns responsibility to the command staff as well as Hitler. Political direction sets out the intended objective, while the staff prepares plans to carry it out. Generals and admirals are also expected to offer professional advice. Within this argument, failure to give that advice and failure to accept it are separate sources of responsibility.

evidence.note: Political direction is distinguished from the command staff's responsibilities for planning and professional advice.

segments.summary: The interpretation distinguishes political direction from the command staff's responsibility for plans and professional advice.

segments.title: Soryu changes Mediterranean carrier operations
segments.body: An additional carrier would change the Mediterranean Fleet's operating tempo. Soryu and Illustrious could work as a pair, with one concentrating on daytime strikes and the other on fighters and air defence. The Victorious-Saratoga comparison illustrates how complementary duties could allow the two air groups to work together while integration develops. Eagle would gain time for overdue maintenance. Three carriers would also let Soryu and Illustrious rotate through upkeep without suspending the fleet's carrier capability. Japanese fighters would ease pressure on the limited Fulmar force, while resources otherwise sent to Australia and Singapore could sustain North Africa and Alexandria.

evidence.note: The Victorious-Saratoga comparison illustrates complementary carrier roles, with Soryu, Illustrious, and Eagle sharing operations and maintenance.
Japanese fighters would reduce demand on Fulmars, while resources formerly needed in the Far East could support North Africa and Alexandria.

segments.summary: Adding Soryu lets Illustrious, Eagle, and the Japanese carrier share maintenance, air defense, strike, and supply burdens in the Mediterranean.

segments.title: American equipment reaches North Africa through the Pacific and Indian Oceans
segments.body: Japanese aircraft operating from British carriers are a possible later development, with rapid adoption considered unlikely while British purchases from the Americans are already being negotiated. American equipment for North Africa could travel across the Pacific and Indian Oceans without entering the Atlantic submarine convoy routes. Ships could sail more regularly where they no longer need to wait for convoy assembly. German merchant raiders would remain a threat, so vulnerable stretches could still require convoys escorted by older British C-, D-, and E-class cruisers. Japanese maritime patrol aircraft could reinforce positions around the Indian Ocean. Cooperation would also give Japan firsthand knowledge of British imperial operations, as its assistance during the First World War had done.

evidence.note: Japanese aircraft aboard British ships remain a possible later development, with immediate adoption considered unlikely.
American supplies could avoid Atlantic submarine routes, while older cruisers and Japanese patrol aircraft counter surface raiders.
Japan's First World War assistance provides a precedent for cooperation and learning about British imperial operations.

segments.summary: A friendly Japan opens a supply route that avoids Atlantic submarine concentrations, although German surface raiders still require escorts and patrol aircraft.

segments.title: Carrier readiness and aircraft numbers reshape the Taranto plan
segments.body: A June announcement of Japanese participation would probably produce a worked-up Mediterranean force by August, leaving further preparation time before Taranto. Three carriers could share operations and maintenance, making an October attack possible instead of the historical November timing. The proposed October date is 21 October, Trafalgar Day. The British and Japanese fighter force comprises four Sea Gladiators, fifteen Fulmars, and twenty-one Zeros. Soryu contributes eighteen Val dive bombers and eighteen Kate torpedo bombers, alongside thirty-six British Swordfish. Optional American participation adds eighteen Brewster Buffaloes, thirty-six Helldivers, and eighteen Devastators, with the American air group modelled around Yorktown's contemporary complement.

evidence.note: Arrival, work-up, maintenance, and the possible 21 October or November timing of the raid.
Proposed British and Japanese aircraft numbers and the optional American air group.

segments.summary: An August arrival gives Japanese ships time to work up before an October or November attack, with larger air groups and optional American reinforcement.

segments.title: Taranto becomes a night-and-dawn carrier blow
segments.body: The proposed Taranto attack begins with thirty-six British Swordfish at night. Fulmars would carry flares and bombs, allowing more Swordfish to concentrate on torpedo attacks. The larger fighter force makes it easier to risk some Fulmars away from fleet defence. A Japanese dawn strike follows, with American aircraft joining only in the version where an American carrier is present. British Fulmars might assist the dawn attack, while Swordfish participation remains uncertain. The sequence is expected to leave little of the Italian fleet operational.

evidence.note: A British Swordfish night attack uses Fulmars for flares and bombs, followed by a Japanese or optional American-Japanese dawn strike.

segments.summary: With Soryu and possibly American carriers present, Taranto becomes a larger British night strike followed by a Japanese or Allied dawn attack.

segments.title: A dawn strike compounds Taranto's damage despite torpedo limitations
segments.body: The historical comparison credits twenty-one Swordfish with disabling three battleships and damaging a heavy cruiser and two destroyers, although some aircraft carried bombs or flares instead of torpedoes. Fifteen additional Swordfish lead to an estimate of four battleships damaged during the counterfactual night attack. Surviving ships would then have to manoeuvre around their damaged sisters while a dawn strike arrived. The American Mark 13 torpedo and Japanese difficulties with harbour attacks remain limitations, with adequate water depth assumed for the Japanese weapons. In the version with American participation, thirty-six torpedo bombers and potentially fifty-four dive bombers would attack with fighter cover. Further hits on already damaged ships would complicate damage control and repairs, leading to a forecast that Italian heavy units would cease to influence operations for twelve to eighteen months. Even a surviving Giulio Cesare is judged insufficient to cover the proposed operations around Crete, Malta, and North Africa.

evidence.note: Historical Taranto damage and the projected effects of additional night attackers followed by a dawn strike.
American and Japanese torpedo limitations, assumed harbour depth, and attacks on manoeuvring or already damaged ships.
The forecast removes Italian heavy units from operations for twelve to eighteen months, even if Giulio Cesare survives.

segments.summary: The proposed follow-up targets damaged battleships and ships leaving harbour, while acknowledging limitations in American torpedoes and Japanese harbour attacks.

segments.title: A greater Taranto defeat threatens Mussolini's authority
segments.body: A larger Taranto defeat is presented as a serious threat to Mussolini's regime without assuming that it would bring the regime down. His responsibilities as minister of both the navy and air force connect the naval disaster directly to his government. Repaired ships and renewed operations historically allowed him to point to recovery after Taranto. The counterfactual removes that opportunity for an extended period and considers the consequences for his authority in Italy and his relationship with Germany.

evidence.note: Mussolini's naval and air responsibilities, the historical recovery of prestige, and the proposed political consequences of prolonged fleet losses.

segments.summary: The counterfactual links a prolonged loss of the battle fleet to Mussolini's ministerial responsibilities and relations with Germany.

segments.title: Sea control isolates North Africa and protects Crete
segments.body: A shattered Italian battle fleet would change where Allied ships and troops were needed. Japanese, Australian, or other Empire formations could sustain the advance in North Africa or reinforce Greece without stripping the original offensive. Cruisers, destroyers, and submarines could attack Axis coastal supply traffic without intervention by Italian heavy ships, potentially ending the North African campaign in February or March 1941. A rapid Axis collapse could also loosen Vichy control in French North Africa and change the leadership of the Free French. In this forecast, Crete remains an Allied air base because the Italians cannot support the amphibious operation. Older battleships would be sufficient to contain a surviving Italian unit, releasing modernized Queen Elizabeth-class ships for Atlantic blocking duties. The larger Allied force could persuade Germany to postpone the twins' January sortie until May, concentrate a stronger force, or abandon the breakout.

evidence.note: Japanese and Dominion troops could reinforce Greece or North Africa while fewer battleships remain in the Mediterranean.
British battleships could take Atlantic blocking positions while Crete remains an Allied air base.
Light forces and reinforced armies could cut North African supply and accelerate the campaign.

segments.summary: With the Italian battle fleet disabled, Allied cruisers, destroyers, submarines, and troops can cut North African supply while heavy ships redeploy north.

segments.title: Slow battleships block Atlantic routes while fast forces hunt raiders
segments.body: The Mediterranean can be closed at either end, while German warships have routes into the North Atlantic through Norway and toward French ports. Reinforcing the Home Fleet therefore remains necessary even after Italian heavy forces are disabled. Queen Elizabeth-class battleships lack the speed to chase Bismarck, but they could occupy positions a raider must pass. Warspite and Valiant together would force a German commander to consider whether any victory would leave enough damage to invite destruction by the next Allied force. Nagato, Mutsu, Nelson, and Rodney add further heavy units, while Kongos and faster British capital ships provide pursuit forces. Greater availability could also permit Hood's planned refit and other maintenance. Force H could reinforce the northern approaches or exchange its fast ships for slower battleships and supporting carriers.

evidence.note: Atlantic geography and modernized Queen Elizabeth-class battleships blocking German routes.
Heavy and fast fleet combinations, possible refits, and alternative Force H assignments.

segments.summary: Warspite and Valiant could guard likely German routes, allowing faster British and Japanese ships to pursue breakouts or receive overdue maintenance.

segments.title: Combined carrier groups hunt German surface raiders
segments.body: In this counterfactual, the pairs hunting German raiders could become groups of four capital ships backed by fast carriers. Two British-Japanese squadrons could each contain two Kongos, a King George V-class battleship, and a Renown-class battlecruiser. An available Hood offers further choices of formation, while American participation could support another squadron. Paired carriers divide the work between British night reconnaissance and strikes and Japanese daytime searches and attacks. Older battleships such as Warspite and Valiant could secure Icelandic approaches and important convoys, freeing the fast formations to manoeuvre. Any German sortie in these circumstances is expected to face repeated air attacks before a surface engagement.

evidence.note: Multinational capital-ship groups combine British night aviation with Japanese daytime operations.
Older battleships could cover Icelandic approaches; Hood's loss illustrates the effect of an exceptional shell hit.
Mixed command arrangements would coordinate air attacks ahead of a surface battle.

segments.summary: Fast Anglo-Japanese squadrons could combine carrier searches, day and night strikes, and heavy surface forces against German raiders.

segments.title: Why skilled Japanese aircrews still need a night-flying training system
segments.body: British success at Taranto would give Japanese aircrews a strong reason to improve their night operations. Skilled pilots alone would not provide the training structure needed to make that change quickly during wartime. Pairing a Japanese carrier with a British carrier offers an immediate division of work. The British carrier would conduct night strikes and reconnaissance, while the Japanese carrier would lead daytime attacks and share daytime searches.

evidence.note: Limits of rapid wartime adaptation in Japanese air-group training, followed by complementary British night and Japanese day carrier roles.

segments.summary: British night operations supply a model for Japanese aviation, but wartime training limits favour pairing carriers with complementary skills.

segments.title: Hood's loss and the limits of comparing fleet strength
segments.body: Hood and Prince of Wales are judged capable of winning many versions of their engagement with Bismarck and Prinz Eugen. Hood's historical loss nevertheless demonstrates how the location of a shell hit can change the result. A favoured explanation has the fatal shell passing through a wave trough. That interpretation is explicitly left open to a better-supported argument. The same possibility of exceptional damage remains relevant when comparing the larger fleets in the counterfactual.

evidence.note: The expected force comparison at Denmark Strait, exceptional damage to Hood, and the provisional wave-trough explanation for the fatal hit.

segments.summary: The Denmark Strait comparison allows for exceptional damage even when one side appears stronger on paper.

segments.title: Mixed command teams coordinate the coalition fleet
segments.body: The proposed command arrangement distributes leadership across the participating navies. A British admiral could lead one group with a Japanese deputy, and a Japanese admiral another with a British deputy. If America joined, an American commander and British deputy could lead a further group. Hood, if available after refit, could serve as the flagship for a senior British officer coordinating the combined forces. These are possible arrangements for holding the coalition together. Its German opponents would be expected to face successive air attacks before a surface battle.

evidence.note: National commanders, deputies from partner navies, and a possible overall commander aboard Hood.
The projected battle sequence places repeated air strikes before a surface engagement.

segments.summary: British and Japanese admirals could command separate groups with deputies from the other navy, while an overall commander coordinates their movements.

segments.title: Naval defeat could remove Mussolini without an invasion
segments.body: The political consequences of Taranto Zero could arrive before an invasion of Italy. The counterfactual considers whether the combined loss of the fleet, defeat in North Africa, and a failed Greek campaign could unseat Mussolini. The king and royalist factions could appeal to the British and Japanese monarchies as restorers of constitutional government and seek to change sides. Neutrality is another option, with Germany lacking a significant troop presence in Italy at this stage. Its acceptance would depend on Britain and Japan. An Italian withdrawal early in 1941 would release more Mediterranean ships for Atlantic blockade and submarine hunting, while leaving German surface ships to face carrier attacks in port.

evidence.note: Fleet losses and defeats in North Africa and Greece could threaten Mussolini's position before an invasion of Italy.
Italian royalists could approach the British and Japanese monarchies, with neutrality as an alternative to changing sides.
Mediterranean forces could reinforce blockade, anti-submarine operations, and carrier attacks on German ships in port.

segments.summary: Losing the battle fleet, North Africa, and Greece could let Italian royalists depose Mussolini and seek neutrality or a new alliance before Allied troops land in Italy.

segments.title: Southern France opens while Germany turns east
segments.body: Within the counterfactual, an Italian withdrawal opens a route into southern France with little naval opposition. Free French, British Empire, and Japanese forces could land there while Germany faced the burden of defending and administering more French territory. Reinforcing that front would also present railway and supply difficulties. An Allied landing in Norway remains unattractive because of its difficult amphibious conditions. Holding Crete would put Romanian oil within bomber range, potentially adding to the pressure for Germany to seek Soviet oil. The projection anticipates an Allied landing in 1942 and American entry after further incidents between neutrality patrols and German forces. By this stage, so many earlier events have changed that the proposed course of the war carries substantial uncertainty.

evidence.note: Southern France as an invasion route, German occupation and railway burdens, Norway's amphibious difficulties, and the possible connection between Romanian oil vulnerability and Barbarossa.
A tentative 1942 landing and projected American entry through further neutrality-patrol incidents, with a warning about distant counterfactual prediction.

segments.summary: Italian withdrawal would expose southern France to an Allied landing, while Crete-based air power could threaten Romanian oil and affect Germany's eastern strategy.

segments.title: Norwegian readiness and the risks of an Allied return
segments.body: Norway offers an unattractive Allied invasion route in this counterfactual because of its difficult amphibious conditions. The interpretation of Germany's historical success gives greater weight to Norwegian failures of preparation than to German amphibious skill. Earlier reserve mobilisation, radio warnings, and support for naval officers are identified as measures that could have made the German operation much harder. Clear orders and prepared deputies would also have reduced hesitation within the Norwegian chain of command.

evidence.note: Norway's amphibious difficulties and an interpretation of the 1940 defeat centred on warnings, mobilisation, and command support.

segments.summary: Norway remains a difficult Allied landing option, while the interpretation of German success in 1940 focuses on Norwegian preparation.

segments.title: More carriers change the Arctic convoy covering force
segments.body: The Soviet Union could receive supplies through the Far East and Iran as well as through Arctic convoys. In the Arctic, the counterfactual makes enough ships available for a heavy covering force of two or three carriers and two or three capital ships or more. German forces that could be based and sustained in Norway are judged insufficient to drive that force away. Submarines would still pose a threat, but the covering force would have more aircraft and other resources to respond. A repetition of the PQ 17 disaster is therefore considered unlikely within this scenario. Together with the wider Allied offensive, this improved supply position forms part of the tentative projection that the war could end during 1943.

evidence.note: Soviet supply routes, a larger Arctic covering force, the remaining submarine threat, and a tentative 1943 end-of-war projection.

segments.summary: The enlarged coalition fleet could protect Soviet supply routes with several carriers and capital ships, changing the conditions behind a PQ 17-type disaster.

segments.title: Crete-based bombers target Romanian oil
segments.body: Crete becomes the proposed base for a bombing offensive against Romanian oil. January 1942 is the chosen start, after the German invasion of the Soviet Union stretches its transport and fuel reserves into winter. The operation requires time to assemble bombers and build the supporting infrastructure. Ships could carry aircraft and supplies along the North African coast, using ports overnight, or take the longer route around Africa to Alexandria. A March 1942 landing in southern France would follow the attacks on fuel production. Italian neutrality would remove the need to invade Italy, while Italian forces committed to the Soviet Union would be dispersed if the country remained at war. The further this projection runs into 1942, the less secure its assumptions become.

evidence.note: January 1942 is the proposed moment to attack Romanian oil, after building bomber strength and infrastructure on Crete.
Coastal or around-Africa shipping routes, a March 1942 landing in southern France, and the reasons for bypassing Italy in this distant projection.

segments.summary: A proposed January 1942 offensive from Crete attacks Romanian oil as German winter fuel reserves fall, followed by a March landing in southern France.

segments.title: Shared combat experience and the risk of a later Pacific war
segments.body: The counterfactual leaves a later Japanese-American war unresolved. Fighting as allies could build military relationships that reduce the risk of conflict. Japanese ground forces serving alongside British and American troops would also see their fighting qualities at first hand, challenging assumptions about an easy opponent. Such experience provides no guarantee against a later strategic crisis or the thinking that could lead Japan into one.

evidence.note: Uncertainty about a later Japanese-American war, relationships formed in common service, and Japanese reassessment of allied ground forces.

segments.summary: Service alongside British and American troops could alter Japanese assessments of their fighting qualities, while the risk of later conflict remains unresolved.

segments.title: Could a mass German breakout beat the coalition fleet?
segments.body: The closing operational problem assumes that Germany holds back its major ships and completes Graf Zeppelin for a mass sortie in August 1941. Bismarck, Tirpitz, Scharnhorst, and Gneisenau would accompany the carrier before America enters the war. Each of two Anglo-Japanese groups would have a British and Japanese carrier, a King George V-class ship, a Renown-class ship, and two Kongos. Nelson, Rodney, Queen Elizabeth-class ships, Nagato, and Mutsu could provide additional heavy or blocking forces. Carrier reconnaissance raises the possibility of concentrating the two groups into four carriers and eight fast capital ships before the Germans arrive. The German ships' battleship construction remains an advantage to consider, but the result of the engagement is left open for viewers to work through.

evidence.note: The open problem assumes an August 1941 German breakout with Graf Zeppelin and four capital ships before American entry.
Two Anglo-Japanese groups, slower blocking forces, possible carrier-led concentration, and the German battleships' construction are factors for an unanswered engagement.

segments.summary: The closing problem pits Bismarck, Tirpitz, Scharnhorst, Gneisenau, and Graf Zeppelin against two Anglo-Japanese carrier groups and a deep blocking force.

segments.title: How commitments against Japan limit the route to Romanian oil
segments.body: Aircraft range and the availability of bases limit attacks on Romanian oil. Securing suitable Mediterranean airfields first requires enough naval strength to contain or defeat the Italian fleet. British forces assigned to watch Japan reduce the strength available for that Mediterranean task. In this counterfactual, changing Japan's alignment alters those deployments and makes the proposed bomber bases possible. The additional force matters through that sequence of commitments and access to bases.

evidence.note: The connection between forces watching Japan, Mediterranean security, bomber-base availability, and aircraft range to Romanian oil.

segments.summary: The closing strategic argument connects British commitments against Japan to Mediterranean sea control and airfields within range of Romanian oil.
